section.title: A Living Hope
section.sectionRationale: After the greeting, Peter bursts into praise. This long sentence of blessing is the engine room of the letter: it announces the new birth, the living hope, and the imperishable inheritance that make suffering bearable. Everything the readers are called to endure is set against the certainty of what God has already secured for them in the risen Christ.
section.thesis: Because God in His great mercy has given us new birth into a living hope and an imperishable inheritance kept safe in heaven, believers rejoice even through fiery trials that prove their faith, receiving the salvation the prophets foretold and the angels long to see.
section.frameNote: Three movements: new birth into a living hope and inheritance, verses 3 to 5; joy and tested faith in trials, verses 6 to 9; and the salvation foretold by prophets and longed for by angels, verses 10 to 12.

units.label: New birth into a living hope

verses.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us {{anagennao|new birth}} into a {{elpis|living hope}} through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
and into an {{kleronomia|inheritance}} that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,
who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the {{soteria|salvation}} that is ready to be revealed in the last time.
In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials
so that the {{dokimion|proven character}} of your faith, more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire, may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
Though you have not seen Him, you love Him; and though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy,
now that you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

units.label: Foretold by prophets, longed for by angels

verses.text: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully,
trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the {{pathemata|sufferings}} of Christ and the glories to follow.

It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things.

anagennao.gloss: To beget again, to give new birth. It describes God bringing a person to spiritual life from above, a fresh beginning that is entirely His doing. Peter says God has caused us to be born again, so that the Christian life starts not with human effort but with God's regenerating mercy.

elpis.gloss: A living hope, a confident expectation that is alive and active because it rests on the risen Christ. Unlike wishful thinking, this hope is guaranteed by the resurrection. It is called living because it draws its life from the living Lord and cannot die or disappoint.

kleronomia.gloss: An inheritance, the possession that belongs to an heir. Peter piles up three words to describe it: imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, and adds that it is kept in heaven. Unlike any earthly estate, this inheritance cannot rot, be spoiled, or fade, for God Himself guards it.

soteria.gloss: Salvation, rescue, deliverance. Peter speaks of it as already possessed yet still to be fully revealed in the last time. It is the goal of faith and the salvation of the soul, God's complete rescue of His people that reaches its climax when Christ appears.

dokimion.gloss: The proving or testing of something, the genuineness that comes out through trial. Like fire refining gold, hardship tests faith and proves it real. The tested, purified faith is more precious than gold and will result in praise, glory, and honor when Jesus is revealed.

pathemata.gloss: Sufferings, the things one undergoes. Peter uses it for the sufferings of Christ that the prophets foretold, followed by the glories. This pattern, suffering then glory, runs through the whole letter and shapes how believers read their own trials, as the road that leads to glory.

basic.context: Peter turns from greeting to praise, and the praise is really the heart of his message to suffering people. God, out of sheer mercy, has given them a brand new life and a hope that cannot die, because Jesus rose from the dead. Waiting for them in heaven is an inheritance that can never rot or fade. So even when trials burn like fire, they can rejoice, because those trials only prove their faith is real. This is the salvation the old prophets strained to see and even angels long to understand.
basic.hermeneutics: Notice the order: praise God for what He has done, then face the trials. Peter does not deny the readers' grief; he says they suffer real sorrow in various trials. But he sets that sorrow inside a far bigger reality, a living hope and a kept inheritance. Trials are for a little while; the inheritance is forever. That perspective is meant to reframe how they, and we, endure.
basic.originalLanguages: God has caused our anagennao, our new birth, into a living elpis, hope, because Jesus is risen. Our kleronomia, inheritance, is imperishable and kept in heaven for the soteria, salvation, soon to be revealed. Trials bring the dokimion, the proving, of faith, more precious than gold. The prophets foretold the pathemata, the sufferings, of Christ and the glories to follow.
basic.typology: The prophets who searched their own words for the sufferings and glories of Christ show the whole Old Testament pointing forward to Him. The imperishable inheritance kept in heaven answers the earthly promised land Israel received, a land that could be lost; the true inheritance never can. And the pattern of suffering then glory in Christ becomes the shape of the believer's own path.
basic.christ: The resurrection of Jesus is the ground of everything here: the new birth, the living hope, the whole salvation. The prophets were pointing to His sufferings and the glories to follow. Believers love and trust a Christ they have not seen, and their salvation is revealed when He appears. He is the risen source of hope and the coming Lord of glory.
basic.god: God is the Father of our Lord Jesus, rich in great mercy. He is the one who gives new birth, guards the inheritance in heaven, and shields His people by His power through faith. He planned this salvation long ago, revealed it through the prophets, and now brings it to His people by the Spirit. He is a merciful, powerful, purposeful God.
basic.crossReferences: James 1 speaks of trials that test and mature faith. Romans 8 speaks of an inheritance and glory that far outweigh present suffering. First Corinthians 15 grounds hope in the resurrection. And Luke 24 shows the risen Christ opening the prophets who spoke of His suffering and glory.
basic.oneStory: The prophets longed to see it, the angels long to look into it, and now these scattered believers are living in it: the salvation God planned from of old, secured by the risen Christ. New birth, living hope, and an unfading inheritance are the present taste of the homecoming the whole Bible has been moving toward.

context.literary:
The praise of verses 3 to 12 is the doorway into the whole letter, and in the Greek it is carried by one very long sentence. It opens with a blessing, Peter piles up relative clauses ('who,' 'in whom,' 'concerning which salvation'), and each clause hands on the thought to the next, so that the reader is carried from the risen Christ to the inheritance, from the inheritance to the trial, from the trial to the prophets and at last to the angels. The effect is a single breath of worship.

The three movements are arranged by direction of time. Verses 3 to 5 look back and forward at once: a birth that has already happened and an inheritance that is waiting. Verses 6 to 9 sit in the present, in trials and in love for an unseen Lord. Verses 10 to 12 look back to the prophets and sideways to the angels, to show how long and how widely this salvation has been awaited. The word 'salvation' appears in verses 5, 9 and 10 and binds the three together, and the mention of 'revelation' in 1:5, 1:7 and 1:13 gives a steady glance toward the end.

There is a pattern of contrasts. Perishable gold is set against imperishable inheritance. 'A little while' is set against forever. 'Now' against 'the last time.' Grief against joy. What the readers have not seen against what they love. The suffering of Christ, in the plural, is set against the glories that follow.

The passage also has its pivot. In verse 6 the Greek begins with 'in this,' which turns from what God has done to how the readers live in it, and the same thing is done again at 1:13 with 'therefore,' where the praise becomes instruction.
context.historical:
The readers are the exiles of the previous verses, living in the provinces of Asia Minor in the 60s of the first century. The trials of verse 6 are real and various, and the letter fills them in: slander, 2:12 and 3:16, the loss of social standing, 4:4, and the prospect of a 'fiery trial,' 4:12. They are not yet facing an empire wide persecution, but they are experiencing the daily, grinding pressure that comes from refusing to share in the life of their neighbours.

Two images from the daily world give the passage its force. The first is inheritance. In the ancient world an inheritance was a family's land, and land could be lost to debt, to conquest or to a swindle, as the story of Naboth shows in 1 Kings 21. Israel itself lost its inheritance in the exile. Peter's three adjectives, imperishable, undefiled and unfading, describe an inheritance that cannot be lost in any of those ways: it cannot be destroyed by war, cannot be corrupted by the unclean and cannot wither by time.

The second image is the refiner's furnace. Gold ore was heated until the dross rose and could be skimmed off, and the Scriptures often use the process of the people of God, as in Proverbs 17:3, Zechariah 13:9 and Psalm 66:10. Peter's point is that even refined gold perishes in the end, while faith that has been through the fire does not.

The prophets in verses 10 and 11 would have been understood by his readers as the writers of the Old Testament. Daniel's own wondering is a good example, for he heard the vision and asked what the outcome would be, only to be told that the words were sealed until the end, Daniel 12:8 and 9.
context.canonical:
The opening blessing is the same Jewish form of praise that Paul uses at the start of Ephesians 1:3 and 2 Corinthians 1:3, and Peter's words are identical to the first of these. The theme of new birth belongs to Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus, John 3:3 to 7, to Paul's 'washing of new birth' in Titus 3:5, and to Peter's own later expansion in 1:23, where it is the living and enduring word that brings it about.

The inheritance and the hope stored up in heaven is paralleled in Colossians 1:5, and the idea that Christ's death opened a promised inheritance for those who are called is in Hebrews 9:15. Paul tells the Ephesians that the Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance, Ephesians 1:14. The teaching that present suffering is small beside coming glory is in Romans 8:17 and 18 and 2 Corinthians 4:17 and 18. Paul traces the same chain, suffering, perseverance, character and hope, in Romans 5:1 to 5, and James opens with the testing of faith in James 1:2 and 3, in the same phrases as Peter in verse 6 and 7.

The verses on the prophets draw on a conviction found across the New Testament that the Scriptures speak of Christ. Jesus Himself told two disciples on the Emmaus road that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and enter His glory, Luke 24:25 to 27 and 44 to 46. Hebrews 1:1 and 2 says that God spoke through the prophets and now speaks by the Son, and 2 Peter 1:19 to 21 says that the prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit. The curiosity of the angels is paralleled in Ephesians 3:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter writes to people who are suffering for their faith and who are tempted to conclude that they must have made a mistake. His aim in these verses is to lift their eyes from the present pain to the reality that surrounds it. The grammar of the passage puts God's act first: He has caused the new birth, He guards the inheritance and He is the one who sent the prophets and the Spirit. The readers are not asked to manufacture hope. They are asked to notice that they already have it, because Jesus is risen.

He also means to answer the question of why. The trials are not accidents and not signs of abandonment. They are part of a process that, like a refiner's fire, shows what is real and results in praise at the appearing of Christ. The phrase 'if need be' in the Greek of verse 6 indicates that the trial has a purpose within God's care. The word for a little while sets the length of the suffering against eternity.

Peter wants his readers to know that they belong to a very large story. The prophets of centuries before searched their own words for it, and the angels still bend to look at it. To a small, unnoticed group in a provincial town, this is a sweeping reassurance of significance.

He also intends them to love Christ. The faith he describes is not a calculation but an unseen love and an inexpressible joy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These verses are overwhelmingly descriptive. They declare what God has done and what the readers now have and experience. There is a single command in the whole passage, implied in the opening, to bless God. Peter will turn to imperatives at verse 13 with 'therefore.'

The description must not be read as a promise that trials will be removed or shortened on a human timetable. 'Little while' is measured against eternity, and the same letter expects suffering to continue, 4:12 to 19 and 5:10. It also does not promise that every believer will feel the joy of verse 8. It describes what is true of them as a group and encourages individuals to look for it.

The passage also does not teach that suffering is good in itself. The point of the refiner's image is the end result, not the fire. Believers are not urged to seek affliction but to trust God in it.

Applied today, the verses are a pattern for how to bring sorrow and joy together in the same heart. They say that grief is real, and that joy rooted in what Christ has done is real too, and that the second can sit alongside the first without cancelling it.

debates.question: Is the believer's salvation past, present or future?

views.label: A future salvation still to be revealed
views.case: Verse 5 speaks of a salvation 'ready to be revealed in the last time,' and the language of inheritance and 'revelation of Jesus Christ' in verse 7 looks to the end. On this reading the new birth is the start and salvation proper is the full deliverance at Christ's appearing, Romans 13:11.

views.label: A present possession
views.case: Verse 9 says the readers are 'receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls,' using a present form of the verb. Peter and Paul can also speak of believers as already saved, Titus 3:5. The salvation is therefore something they now enjoy, and the hope is that it will be completed.

views.label: Both, already and not yet
views.case: Most interpreters hold that Peter deliberately holds both. The new birth and the cleansing are done, the Spirit is given, and the final revelation is still ahead. The pattern runs through the New Testament, in Romans 8:23 and 24 and Ephesians 1:13 and 14, where the Spirit is a pledge of what is still to come.

debates.bearing: The third reading best explains why Peter can use both a future and a present verb in the same paragraph, and it gives believers a way to live in the tension between joy now and glory later.

debates.question: Does being 'shielded' mean a believer cannot fall away?

views.label: God's power guarantees perseverance
views.case: The participle in verse 5 pictures God's power as a garrison around His people, and the inheritance is 'reserved in heaven.' Reformed interpreters conclude that all those who are born again will be kept to the end, and that the faith that endures is itself God's gift. Passages such as Philippians 4:7, where God's peace 'will guard' the heart, use the same verb.

views.label: The shielding works through faith that must continue
views.case: Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters stress the phrase 'through faith.' God's power guards those who continue to trust, and the letter's warnings, 4:17 to 19 and 5:8 to 9, suggest a real danger of turning away. Perseverance is therefore a response, not an automatic result.

views.label: A shield for believers, not a measure of anyone's heart
views.case: Others argue that the verse is not meant to settle the question of who in particular will persevere. Peter is encouraging people who are already trusting, and says that God's power and their faith are both at work. The passage then is for comfort, and should not be used to speculate about others.

debates.bearing: All three agree that those who trust in Christ have God's power on their side and that the believer's part is to keep trusting, which is what Peter intends.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of note is the verb for new birth, anagennao, 'to beget again.' Peter is the only New Testament writer who uses it, here and in verse 23, and he applies it to God as the begetter. It is close to the idea of being 'born again' in John 3:3 and Titus 3:5, which calls it the 'washing of new birth.' The tense is an aorist participle, pointing to a completed act at a point in time, while the hope it produces is called living, zosa, meaning alive and life giving, because it rests on the living Christ.

The inheritance is described with three adjectives that begin with the same letter, which is lost in English: aphtharton, amianton and amaranton. Each carries the negative prefix, 'not perishable,' 'not defiled,' 'not fading.' The sound itself gives a sense of a thing that resists decay, stain and the passing of time. The verb 'reserved,' tereo, is in the perfect tense, which says that it has been kept and remains kept.

Verse 5 gives the other side with a different verb. The readers are 'shielded,' phroureo, a military word for guarding or garrisoning. It is used in 2 Corinthians 11:32 of the governor who 'secured' Damascus with guards and in Philippians 4:7 of God's peace that 'will guard your hearts.' The present tense means that the guarding is continuing. God keeps the inheritance for them and keeps them for the inheritance.

The rejoicing in verses 6 and 8 uses agalliao, a word of exultant, almost celebratory joy. Jesus uses it in Matthew 5:12, 'Rejoice and be glad,' for those persecuted for His sake. The phrase 'trials of many kinds' in verse 6 is poikilois peirasmois, word for word what James has in James 1:2.

The 'proven character' of verse 7 is dokimion, a testing or the result of testing, and the same expression 'the dokimion of your faith' is in James 1:3. The idea is that the faith is shown to be genuine, as metal is tested to prove it pure.

In verse 11 the prophets were looking into the 'sufferings,' pathemata, of Christ and the glories that follow, both in the plural. Verse 12 closes with the angels, who 'long to look,' parakypto, which means to bend over in order to see, the verb used of someone stooping to peer into the tomb in John 20:5 and 11, and also of looking intently into the law in James 1:25.

typology.type: The inheritance of the land and the inheritance in heaven
typology.fulfillment: Israel's inheritance was the promised land, divided by lot and held as a gift from the Lord, Psalm 16:5 and 6. Yet the land could be lost, and was, in the exile, and even in its best days it was God's land and they were guests, Leviticus 25:23. Peter's inheritance is the fulfilment the land had always pointed toward: the promise to Abraham was an inheritance, Galatians 3:18, and Christ, the mediator of a new covenant, has opened it to those who are called, Hebrews 9:15. The escalation is from a patch of earth to a place that is imperishable, and from a possession that could be taken to one that is kept in heaven, with the Spirit as a pledge, Ephesians 1:14.

The Old Testament speaks repeatedly of God refining His people like silver and gold, Zechariah 13:9, Psalm 66:10 and Isaiah 48:10, and says that the Lord is the tester of hearts, Proverbs 17:3. The image reaches its fullest meaning in Christ, who endured the ultimate trial and came through to glory, so that the believer's testing is a sharing in His path, Romans 8:17. The type falls short at one point: the fire that tested Christ was not to remove impurities, since He had none, but to bear ours, 1 Peter 2:24. The believer's refinement has the marks of grace, and Peter says it will result in praise and honour at His appearing.

typology.type: The prophets who searched and served
typology.fulfillment: The prophets spoke of a salvation they did not see, and puzzled over it, as Daniel did, Daniel 12:8 and 9. They were told they were serving a later generation. Jesus confirmed the pattern after His resurrection by explaining to two disciples what the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms said about Him, Luke 24:25 to 27. Hebrews 1:1 and 2 sets the prophets and the Son in sequence. The escalation is that what they strained to see has now been announced in the gospel, and the Spirit who spoke through them has been sent from heaven. The type falls short only in that the prophets saw it dimly and the apostles saw it from the other side of the resurrection.

typology.type: The gold that perishes and the faith that does not
typology.fulfillment: Peter compares faith with gold, the most valued metal, and says that even gold, which is refined by fire, will eventually perish. The comparison is a way of pointing to the surpassing worth of faith in Christ and to the fact that the things which the world tests and values pass away, while the proven faith results in praise at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Paul draws the same contrast between the temporary and the eternal in 2 Corinthians 4:17 and 18. The correspondence has its limit: faith is not itself the treasure, as if believers earned the inheritance by it. Faith is the means by which they receive the one who is.

study.christ:
The resurrection of Jesus is the ground of everything in the passage. The living hope comes 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,' and the whole chain of new birth, inheritance and shielded salvation hangs from that event. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and Peter's thought is the same: because the first sheaf has been gathered, the harvest is certain. A hope that rests on a dead teacher could only be wishful, but a hope that rests on a living Lord is a living hope.

The prophets' searching shows a second way in which the passage leads to Christ. They were looking at His 'sufferings' and 'the glories to follow,' and the order and the plural are deliberate. Jesus taught the same order on the road to Emmaus when He asked whether it was not necessary for the Christ to suffer and then enter His glory, Luke 24:26. Peter's phrase 'the Spirit of Christ in them' also says something about who Christ is: He was at work in the Old Testament prophets, which reflects His existence before His coming and the unity of the Old and New Testaments, as 1:20 and 2 Peter 1:21 also suggest.

Christ is the unseen object of the believer's love. 'Though you have not seen Him, you love Him' is an echo of what He said to Thomas, 'blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed,' John 20:29. Peter himself had seen the Lord and been restored by Him, so he writes as someone who knows what it is to love Him and what the love costs.

He is also the one who will be revealed. Verse 7 looks to 'the revelation of Jesus Christ,' and verse 13 will tell the readers to set their hope fully on the grace to be given them at that time. His return is the day on which the proven faith of every believer is shown to be genuine and praised.

A word of care is needed. The refiner's fire is not itself Christ, and the prophets' searching is not a code the reader must crack. The links hold where the text makes them, in the resurrection as the ground, in the sufferings and glories as the pattern, and in the love of the unseen Lord as the believer's response.
study.god:
The passage opens with God named by His relation to Jesus Christ, 'the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,' and the first thing said about Him is that He is to be blessed. Everything that follows is praise for what He has done, and that gives the theology of the passage its character. Peter is not building an argument about God's attributes. He is celebrating a God whose character is shown in His actions.

He is merciful. The new birth comes 'by His great mercy,' which means that it is not earned and that the one receiving it has nothing to offer. Mercy is God's response to people in need, and Peter says it is great, an echo of the way God described Himself to Moses as abounding in loving devotion, Exodus 34:6.

He is powerful and protective. The readers are guarded by His power, and the inheritance is kept by Him. The picture is of a God who both prepares and defends, who has made a place for them and who is garrisoning them on the way to it. Believers are not left to hold on by their own strength.

He is purposeful. The trials have a place in His plan, since they are 'if need be' and have a result in praise and glory. The prophets served a plan that He set in motion long before, and the Spirit has been at work in the whole of it. Nothing in the passage is accidental, and God does not appear as a bystander to His people's suffering but as one who is working for them in it.

He is a God of joy. The result of His work in believers is an 'inexpressible and glorious joy.' He does not simply rescue them from the pit. He fills them with a joy that exceeds what words can express.

It is also worth noticing that the whole Trinity is present, the Father who gives birth, the Son who rose, and the Spirit through whom the gospel was preached. For worship, the right response is the one Peter begins with: to bless God, before and after the troubles, because of what He has done.

crossReferences.note: Paul begins with the same words as Peter, 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,' and goes on to praise the God who chose us before the foundation of the world. The two apostles lead their letters with the same doxology, which shows how basic praise is to the Christian message.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, of water and the Spirit. Peter's new birth is the same event seen from the Father's side, as a gift of God and not a human achievement.

When the kindness of God appeared, He saved us through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, so that we become heirs with the hope of eternal life. In one sentence Paul links the new birth, mercy, the Spirit, hope and inheritance, just as Peter does in verses 3 to 5.

The Spirit is described as the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession. It explains how an inheritance 'reserved in heaven' can be known now: the Spirit is a down payment and guarantee of what is waiting.

Paul says that heirs of God suffer with Christ so as to be glorified with Him, and that present sufferings are not comparable to the glory to be revealed. This is Peter's thought in verses 6 and 7, that trial and glory belong to the same road.

A light and momentary affliction produces an eternal glory beyond comparison, and believers fix their eyes on what is unseen. It matches Peter's contrast of a little while with forever, and his picture of believers loving one they cannot see.

James tells his readers to count trials of many kinds as joy, because the testing of faith produces perseverance. Peter's words about various trials and the proving of faith are almost the same, which suggests that this was common teaching in the early church.

The Lord promises to bring His people through the fire and refine them like silver and test them like gold, so that they will call on His name and He will answer. It is the Old Testament picture behind Peter's refining of faith, and it ends with relationship restored.

The risen Jesus explains to two disciples that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and enter His glory, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. It is the clearest New Testament statement of what Peter says the prophets were searching for in verses 10 and 11.

Daniel hears a vision and asks what the outcome will be, and is told that the words are sealed until the time of the end. It is a concrete case of a prophet who did not understand the time of what he wrote, and shows what Peter means when he says that the prophets searched and investigated.

Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Peter's living hope depends on this fact, and the image of firstfruits explains why His resurrection guarantees ours: the harvest has begun.

Jesus tells Thomas that those who have not seen and yet have believed are blessed. Peter's readers have never seen the Lord, yet love Him and believe, and Peter applies this beatitude to them with an unusual note of warmth.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a good creation that was spoiled by sin, and almost every page that follows is an effort of God to bring a good ending out of that loss. This passage is Peter's summary of the ending, put in the past tense for what has happened and the future tense for what is coming. The turn on which the whole story swings is the resurrection of Jesus, and the living hope is the confidence that the story will end as He has shown it can.

The Old Testament supplies the longing. The promised land was a first, partial installment of an inheritance that could be lost, and the exile showed the weakness of any earthly arrangement. The prophets spoke of a salvation they could not see, of a Servant who would suffer and then be exalted, and of a new heart and a new Spirit. The sufferings and the glories were both in their writings and they never saw how the two fitted. Peter says that they now do: the Christ suffered first, and glory followed.

The New Testament gives the answer. The Son has come, been put to death and raised, and the Spirit has been sent from heaven, and the gospel has been proclaimed to people such as these readers. Their new birth, their inheritance and their joy under trial are all the fruit of that sequence. They live now between the resurrection and the revelation, in the stretch of time in which faith is tested and love for an unseen Lord is proven.

The story ends in the new creation, where hope is no longer needed because what was hoped for has come. Revelation 21:1 to 4 speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, the dwelling of God with His people and the end of death and mourning, and 22:3 says there will no longer be any curse. The inheritance that was kept in heaven comes down, and those who believed without seeing see Him. Every trial of the present is then understood as what Peter said it was, for a little while, and the faith that passed through the fire is found to be to the praise and glory and honour of Jesus Christ.

quiz.q: On what is the living hope grounded?

options.text: The resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.
options.note: Verse 3: the hope is living because it rests on the risen Christ.

options.text: God's great mercy toward His people.
options.note: True, mercy gives the new birth, but the hope is specifically grounded in the resurrection.

options.text: The strength of the believer's own faith.
options.note: Faith receives the hope; it does not create or ground it.

options.text: The promise of an easier life now.
options.note: Peter frankly expects trials; the hope is fixed on the inheritance to come.

quiz.q: How does Peter describe the inheritance kept for believers?

options.text: Imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven.
options.note: Verse 4: three words for what no earthly inheritance can be, and it is guarded by God.

options.text: A reward we must work hard to keep from losing.
options.note: It is kept in heaven by God's power, not held by our effort.

options.text: A blessing enjoyed fully now with nothing left to come.
options.note: It is reserved in heaven, awaiting the salvation to be revealed.

options.text: A secure future possession we await with hope.
options.note: True to the sense, though it understates the threefold description of its perfection.

quiz.q: Why can believers rejoice even in various trials?

options.text: Because trials prove their faith genuine, more precious than gold, unto praise when Christ appears.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7: the refining fire purifies faith for glory.

options.text: Because the trials are only for a little while.
options.note: True and comforting, though the deeper reason is what the trials accomplish in proving faith.

options.text: Because suffering earns them their salvation.
options.note: Salvation is God's merciful gift; trials prove faith, they do not purchase salvation.

options.text: Because God has promised to remove all their hardship now.
options.note: Peter expects real grief in trials; the joy is set on the coming glory.

quiz.q: What did the prophets foretell about the Christ?

options.text: His sufferings and the glories to follow.
options.note: Verse 11: the Spirit of Christ pointed to suffering then glory.

options.text: Only His future reign in glory.
options.note: They foretold the sufferings first, then the glories; both together.

options.text: The grace to come, though its details stayed hidden even from them.
options.note: True, they searched carefully, yet the specific content was the sufferings and glory of Christ.

options.text: That salvation would be for themselves alone.
options.note: It was revealed they served not themselves but the readers.

quiz.q: What does it show that even angels long to look into this salvation?

options.text: The gospel is so glorious that the church stands at the center of God's unfolding plan.
options.note: Verse 12: angels themselves strain to grasp the salvation now proclaimed.

options.text: Angels are unsure whether the plan will succeed.
options.note: Their longing is wonder at its glory, not doubt about its outcome.

options.text: The salvation is a small matter of interest to a few.
options.note: The opposite: it draws the gaze of heaven itself.

options.text: Heaven is deeply invested in what God is doing among His people.
options.note: True to the wonder, though it understates how central the church's salvation is to the whole plan.

questions: Peter says God gave you new birth into a living hope. When your circumstances feel dead or hopeless, how does a hope grounded in the risen Christ change what you expect?
Your inheritance is kept in heaven where it cannot fade. Where are you investing yourself in things that can be lost, and how might this reshape your priorities?
Trials are said to prove faith more precious than gold. Can you look back on a hard season and see how it refined and proved your faith?
You love and trust a Christ you have never seen. What feeds that love for Jesus in you, and what tends to dull it?
Prophets longed to see, and angels long to look into, the salvation you now enjoy. How does that lift your sense of what you have been given in the gospel?

translationNotes.note: New birth translates anagennao; a footnote allows has caused us to be born again or has begotten us again, all stressing God as the author of the new life.
The clause more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire, is a parenthesis comparing tested faith to refined gold.
The Spirit of Christ in the prophets predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow, fixing the pattern of suffering then glory that shapes the letter.
